p: Years later, at a dinner party in Washington, two men were introduced and recognized each other simultaneously.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “Gordon and Barlow”, paragraph 8 of 11

p: It was Gordon. It was Barlow.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “Gordon and Barlow”, paragraph 9 of 11

p: They had both assumed the other was dead. They became friends. Gordon told the story many times in his postwar lectures — the enemy officer he had cared for on the field at Gettysburg, the man he had thought was dying, sitting across a dinner table from him in the nation's capital.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “Gordon and Barlow”, paragraph 10 of 11

p: 'We became fast friends,' Gordon wrote, 'and so we shall remain while we both live.'

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “Gordon and Barlow”, paragraph 11 of 11

p: Daniel Sickles was a politician, a killer, and — in his own estimation — a military genius. He had shot his wife's lover on the steps of the White House and been acquitted by reason of temporary insanity — the first successful use of that defense in American legal history. He had wangled a general's commission despite no military training whatsoever. He had survived every disaster through audacity, charm, and a complete inability to recognize that he might be wrong.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “Sickles Moves Forward”, paragraph 1 of 10

p: On the morning of July 2, 1863, he stared at the ground his corps had been assigned and decided it was unsuitable. The Peach Orchard, a quarter-mile to the west along the Emmitsburg Road, sat on slightly higher ground. In Sickles's judgment, the Peach Orchard was the position he should hold.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “Sickles Moves Forward”, paragraph 2 of 10

p: He did not ask Meade. He did not request permission. He did not inform his commander.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “Sickles Moves Forward”, paragraph 3 of 10

p: Around 3:00 in the afternoon, Sickles moved his entire corps — 10,000 men and dozens of artillery pieces — forward to the Emmitsburg Road.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “Sickles Moves Forward”, paragraph 4 of 10

p: Meade discovered the movement and rode south in fury. He found Sickles sitting on horseback in the new line and demanded an explanation. Sickles began to explain. Meade interrupted: the position was untenable. The line was too long. The flanks were exposed. The corps should go back.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “Sickles Moves Forward”, paragraph 5 of 10

p: At that moment, Longstreet's guns opened fire.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “Sickles Moves Forward”, paragraph 6 of 10

p: 'I will withdraw if you order it,' Sickles said.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “Sickles Moves Forward”, paragraph 7 of 10

p: 'I do order it,' Meade replied. 'But the enemy will not allow you to.'

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “Sickles Moves Forward”, paragraph 8 of 10

p: He was right. Within the hour, the Peach Orchard would become the most violent piece of ground on the continent.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “Sickles Moves Forward”, paragraph 9 of 10

p: Sickles lost his right leg to an artillery shell that afternoon. He was carried from the field smoking a cigar — a gesture for his men. He spent the rest of his life, another fifty years, insisting that his unauthorized advance had saved the Army of the Potomac by drawing Confederate attention away from Little Round Top. Most historians disagree. But Sickles never changed his story.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “Sickles Moves Forward”, paragraph 10 of 10

p: The sharpshooters of Berdan's regiment were the best shots in the Union Army. Recruited for their marksmanship, equipped with Sharps repeating rifles, dressed in green uniforms that made them harder to see in the woods — they were an elite within an army that still largely fought in shoulder-to-shoulder lines.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)

p: On the morning of July 2, Sickles was worried about his left. Buford's cavalry had departed. There was open ground stretching south and west, and nobody knew what was on the other side of Pitzer's Woods on Seminary Ridge.
